title: A Bridge for the Harbor
premise: In 1914 coastal England, Elodie Vane has spent fifteen years as driver and gatekeeper for suffragist Lady Rosamund Hale, reading letters and mastering the silences that protect her household. When a census taker's probing questions expose a hidden thread in the Hales' past, Elodie discovers a promise Lady Rosamund made before the war: safe passage and funds for a German-born friend now declared an enemy alien. As authorities close in and Lady Rosamund's own son seeks to use the scandal to seize the family estate, Elodie must choose between loyalty to her employer and the promise itself. In the end, Elodie forges the documents herself, smuggles the friend onto a neutral-bound ship from the harbor, and accepts banishment from the house she served — inheriting instead the truth, and the cost of keeping it.
about_author: Jude Iversen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing domestic correspondence from the Edwardian era. They write historical fiction about the people history recorded only in margins.

chapters.title: The Question on the Form
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. During the 1911-style census enumeration at Hale House, a persistent census taker notices an extra name struck through in an old ledger Elodie is asked to fetch. The beat is quiet dread — fifteen years of careful silence developing its first hairline crack.

chapters.title: Letters Before Breakfast
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, with flashback to 1899 when she first arrived as a girl and learned to read post over the kitchen table. We see how she earned Lady Rosamund's trust and what 'keeping people safe' has cost her personally. Emotional beat: tenderness shadowed by complicity.

chapters.title: The Name in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Lady Rosamund's POV. She confesses the struck-through name: Greta Lindqvist, half-German, once her closest ally in the movement, to whom she promised refuge and money 'if it ever comes to war.' Beat: guilt passed like an inheritance.

chapters.title: The Son Who Counts
chapters.summary: POV of Miles Hale, the heir, home on leave and nursing grievances over his inheritance. He finds the census taker's follow-up letter and begins his own quiet investigation. Beat: ambition curdling into menace; power learning it can be taken.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Knows
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She travels to the harbor town where Greta hides under a false name, working in a fish-packing shed. Their first meeting is wary, transactional — until Greta reveals she knows things about Lady Rosamund that could destroy or save them all. Beat: uneasy alliance.

chapters.title: Papers and Prices
chapters.summary: Alternating Elodie and Miles POVs. Elodie approaches a forger whose fee is information; Miles offers the census taker a bribe dressed as patriotism. Both learn the same lesson: everything in wartime has a price, and someone always sets it. Beat: moral erosion on both sides.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. Authorities raid the packing shed following an anonymous tip — Miles's doing. Greta escapes through the smokehouse but loses her forged papers, and Elodie must decide whether to burn her own correspondence with Lady Rosamund. Beat: terror, sacrifice, point of no return.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Hale House
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She returns to find Miles has told Lady Rosamund he'll expose the promise unless she signs the estate over early. Mother and son face each other; Elodie interrupts with the truth about what Miles tipped off. Beat: the corruption of power made flesh at the family table.

chapters.title: A Bridge for the Harbor
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, climax. Using papers she forges herself and a fisherman who owes Lady Rosamund a debt from the suffrage years, Elodie moves Greta through fog to a neutral-bound ship, nearly caught by Miles at the quay. Beat: breathless courage; the promise kept at last.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, epilogue a year later. Lady Rosamund, having disinherited Miles, offers Elodie partnership in a new venture — but Elodie chooses independence, taking only a letter of introduction and the truth she now carries. Beat: bittersweet freedom; survival's price paid, and worth it.
